title: MCP Agent Fine tuning Workshop - Ronan McGovern

primary.label: Post-Training & Continual Learning
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The workshop's central activity is supervised fine-tuning of a Qwen3 model using LoRA adapters on MCP agent reasoning traces, with explicit discussion of SFT preceding RL. The content targets developers building tool-calling agents and is not specific to any application vertical. The workshop covers trace generation, data cleanup and unrolling, LoRA fine-tuning, pre/post benchmarking, and model deployment to Hugging Face Hub. Requires familiarity with LLMs, fine-tuning concepts, and tool-calling protocols. Hands-on workshop with live demonstrations of agent runs, training, and inference.

summary:
This is a hands-on workshop on MCP agent fine-tuning by Ronan McGovern from Trellis Research, presented at AI Worlds Fair 2025. Students learn to run an agent with MCP tool access, generate high-quality reasoning traces, save multi-turn logs, and fine-tune a Qwen3 model on those traces. MCP (Model Context Protocol) provides LLMs access to tools—specifically Playwright browser automation, though MCPs exist for Stripe, GitHub, Gmail, and more. The LLM is exposed as an OpenAI-style API endpoint with three integration points: converting MCP tool information to JSON, converting tool responses, and detecting tool calls in Hermes format (used even for Qwen models). The prompt uses XML tool call tags containing JSON.

Data generation uses Qwen3 30B (3B activated, MoE) on RunPod via vLLM with reasoning parser and Hermes tool parser. Traces are saved with a tools list (26 browser tools) and a messages list containing full conversation history including thinking tokens. A complex demo navigates trellis.com, handles dropdowns and new tabs. Traces contain noise; manual cleanup and system prompts (not included in training data) guide behavior. Data is unrolled into multiple training rows (3 turns → 3 rows) and pushed to Hugging Face Hub. The demo dataset has 4 examples unrolled to 9.

Fine-tuning uses a modified Unsloth notebook. The 4B Qwen3 model is loaded in 16-bit precision. The chat template converts tools and messages into a single long text string, which the trainer uses. LoRA adapters (rank 32) are applied to attention modules and MLP layers using rescaled LoRA. Training uses batch size 1, one epoch, no warmup steps, AdamW 8-bit optimizer, and constant learning rate. Only 1.62% of parameters are trained; main weights are frozen. Peak memory usage was 75%. The pre-training benchmark shows the 4B model can handle simple tasks but struggles with multi-step ones. Post-training inference confirms the model correctly calls tools. Ronan recommends SFT before RL (GRPO), noting that starting RL without domain-specific SFT causes the model to rarely reach correct answers. He suggests 50-100 curated traces can yield significant improvements for narrow use cases. The trained model can be saved, merged to 16 bits, and pushed to Hugging Face Hub, then dropped into a RunPod pod as an inference endpoint.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Workshop Introduction and Overview
sections.summary: Ronan McGovern introduces the workshop on MCP agent fine-tuning. Students will learn to generate high-quality MCP agent reasoning traces, save tools and multi-turn traces, fine-tune a Qwen3 model, and run the fine-tuned model. Materials are in the Trellis Research AI Worlds Fair 2025 repo under MCP agent fine-tune.

sections.title: MCP Overview and Integration Points
sections.summary: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is defined as a protocol for providing services (tool access) to LLMs. Focus is on browser use via Playwright, though MCPs exist for Stripe, GitHub, Gmail, etc. MCP stores tool information and runs tools. The LLM is exposed as an OpenAI-style endpoint with three integration points: converting tool info to JSON, converting tool responses, and detecting tool calls in Hermes format.

sections.title: Prompt Structure Explanation
sections.summary: A pseudo prompt is shown illustrating the structure: a system message with tool call instructions using XML tags containing JSON, followed by user messages and assistant responses that may include thinking tokens and tool calls. The LLM is told to return function calls as JSON inside tool call tags.

sections.title: Repository and RunPod Setup
sections.summary: The repo is cloned into Windsurf. The README has data collection and fine-tuning sections. Data generation uses Qwen3 30B (3B activated, MoE) on RunPod via a vLLM Docker image with reasoning parser, max model length 32,000, port 8000, automatic tool choice, and Hermes tool parser. Consistency between data generation and fine-tuning models is recommended; OpenAI models are avoided because they don't share thinking traces.

sections.title: Running the Agent Demo
sections.summary: The agent is run with the configured base URL and a truncate argument for tool responses. UV sync is used for dependencies. Playwright provides 25 tools. The demo shows navigating to trellis.com and reading the top two lines, with the browser in non-headless mode and built-in tool call approval. Guidance on tool counts: 25-50 for open-source models, ~200 for Claude.

sections.title: Trace Logging and Data Structure
sections.summary: Saved logs from the demo are reviewed, showing two parts: a tools list (26 browser tools including close, resize, etc.) and a messages list with the full conversation history. The assistant's thinking, tool calls, tool responses (truncated accessibility traces), and final answer are visible. It would not make sense to fine-tune the same model that generated traces; instead, a smaller model lacking this capability is the target.

sections.title: Complex Demo and Trace Cleanup
sections.summary: A more complex task is run: navigate to trellis.com, find the third product (training and fine-tuning), open it in a new tab (tricky for navigation), switch tabs, and read the features section. The agent handles dropdowns and new tabs correctly. Traces contain noise; strategies include manual cleanup (deleting/combining user turns) and using system prompts to guide behavior directly. System prompts need not be included in training data—the goal is clean traces.

sections.title: Pushing Data to Hugging Face Hub and Unrolling
sections.summary: Data is pushed to Hugging Face Hub using push_to_hub with a repo ID and unroll option. Unrolling splits multi-turn conversations into multiple training rows (3 turns → 3 rows: all turns, first 2, first 1), giving more data. This matters because the Qwen template only includes reasoning from the most recent turn. The demo dataset has 4 examples unrolled to 9. Dataset fields include ID, timestamp, model, messages, tools, and a truncation/unrolling flag. A Hugging Face token with write permissions is required.

sections.title: Agent Code Overview
sections.summary: A brief tour of the agent code shows server management (booting MCP servers at startup), schema conversion (MCP to OpenAI and back), tool execution, result wrapping for OpenAI format, tool discovery, the chat loop, reasoning parsing (separate from assistant content), and trace logging helpers.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning Setup with Unsloth
sections.summary: The fine-tuning notebook (based on a modified Unsloth notebook) is opened. Unsloth is installed. The 4 billion parameter Qwen3 model is loaded in 16-bit precision with a large max sequence length. LoRA adapters (not full parameters) will be used but are not applied yet—first, the dataset (9 rows) is loaded and inference is run as a pre-fine-tuning benchmark. A free GPU may not handle larger models; RunPod offers a one-click fine-tuning template.

sections.title: Dataset Inspection and Chat Template
sections.summary: The dataset format is inspected by printing the zeroth row's messages and tools. The chat template is explained: it takes tools and messages and converts them into a single long string. The template can also be found on Hugging Face in the model's tokenizer config. The formatted string starts with a system message, lists all 26 tools, then includes user messages, assistant messages, tool calls, etc. The dataset has 9 rows with the longest at 18,000 tokens, under the 32,000 max length.

sections.title: Pre-Fine-Tuning Benchmark Inference
sections.summary: Before training, inference is run on the first row (navigate to trellis.com) using the raw 4B model. The model should be capable of tool calling, but 26 tools is a lot for a 4B model. It may produce extensive thinking and either call a tool correctly or hit the token limit. The 4B model handles simple tasks but struggles with multi-step tasks, unlike the 30B model which already had difficulty.

sections.title: LoRA Adapter Application and Training Configuration
sections.summary: LoRA adapters are applied to attention modules and MLP layers with rank 32. Rescaled LoRA adjusts the learning rate based on adapter size (larger adapters get lower learning rates). Training uses the prepared text field from the chat template, batch size 1 (due to VRAM limits; A40 or H100 would allow larger), one epoch, no warmup steps, AdamW 8-bit optimizer, and constant learning rate. Only 1.62% of parameters are trained; main weights are frozen. Device memory is 15 GB with 10 GB reserved.

sections.title: Training Execution and Results
sections.summary: Training runs for 9 steps (one epoch). The loss is bumpy due to batch size 1 but generally falls. Peak memory usage is 75%. For production, an eval set, more data (a few hundred traces), TensorBoard logging, and larger batch sizes are recommended. After training, the model can be saved and pushed to Hugging Face Hub, merged to 16 bits, and dropped into a RunPod pod as an inference endpoint.

sections.title: Reinforcement Learning Sidebar
sections.summary: Ronan discusses RL (GRPO) as a related approach. He strongly recommends starting with manual traces and SFT before RL, because a model without domain-specific SFT will struggle to generate correct traces and rarely see positive rewards. For GRPO, rewards require verifiable answers—e.g., navigating to obscure pages and checking against ground truth text. SFT on high-quality traces first speeds up subsequent RL training significantly.

sections.title: Post-Training Inference and Closing
sections.summary: Post-training inference confirms the fine-tuned model correctly calls the expected tool. Recommended inference parameters for Qwen reasoning models include temperature 0.6. Ronan encourages more elaborate evaluation by running the model on an endpoint and testing rollouts in Windsurf. He suggests 50-100 curated traces can yield significant improvements for narrow use cases. Materials are in the Trellis Research AI Worlds Fair 2025 repo, and two MCP videos on the Trellis Research YouTube channel provide more detail on custom MCP servers.
